candidates.text: The rock was wet everywhere else — slick with spray, skinned with weed — but the stone framing the door was dry as a bone, and the brass hinges were polished bright, as though someone had come along with a rag and an oil can and kept them free of rust. He had walked this path every evening for nineteen years and he knew every hollow and loose stone in it; he would have sworn there was nothing here but cliff. Yet the door stood in the rock face like a mouth, six feet high, its panels plain, its threshold worn to a shallow groove in the middle, as if a great many feet had passed over it and gone down. Above him the lamp room stood dark, and the sun was dropping toward the water like a coin slipped into a slot; the wick wanted trimming, the reservoir wanted filling, and the fog would come in on the tide as it always did. But the air breathing out from under the door was warm. It smelled of lamp oil and hot metal, and beneath that, faintly, of the sea — though the sea lay two hundred feet below the path and no tide was running. He set down his can, and laid his palm flat against the wood, and the wood was warm too.

instruction: Answer the brief as you normally would.

task.brief: A lighthouse keeper finds a door in the cliff below the lamp room that was not there yesterday. Write the next paragraph.
good_idea_qualities: the door implies a consequence the keeper must act on
the paragraph keeps the sea and the lamp in view
something is at stake for the keeper personally
task.reference_text: The keeper set the oil can down and counted the door twice, the way he counted ships. It was blue, salt-blistered, and hinged on the seaward side, which meant whoever built it had worked from the water.
